questions.stem:
Statements: All cats are dogs. All dogs are animals.
Conclusions: I. All cats are animals. II. Some animals are cats.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.option_text: Only I follows (All cats→dogs→animals: I follows. Since all cats are animals, some animals are cats: II also follows)
Only II follows (I also follows as shown)
Both I and II follow (correct: I: All cats→dogs→animals; II: since all cats are animals → some animals are cats ✓)
Neither follows (both clearly follow from universal affirmatives)

questions.explanation: C is correct. All A→B, All B→C → All A→C (I follows). Since All cats are animals, by conversion of universal affirmative: Some animals are cats (II follows). When 'All A are B', we can conclude 'Some B are A' by converse.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some books are pens. No pen is a pencil.
Conclusions: I. Some books are not pencils. II. No book is a pencil.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.option_text: Only I follows (correct: Some books are pens + No pen is pencil → Some books are not pencils (I follows). But 'No book is pencil' cannot be concluded because some books may not be pens and could be pencils ✓)
Only II follows (II is too strong — can't conclude ALL books are not pencils)
Both follow (II doesn't follow — see above)
Neither follows (I clearly follows via the particular negative conclusion)

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Some books are pens' + 'No pen is pencil' → at minimum 'Some books (those that are pens) are not pencils' — so I follows. But we can't say ALL books are not pencils, because books that are NOT pens could still be pencils. II ('No book is pencil') doesn't follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: All flowers are trees. Some trees are houses.
Conclusions: I. Some flowers are houses. II. Some houses are trees.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (I: All flowers are trees + Some trees are houses does NOT guarantee some flowers are houses — the 'some trees' that are houses may not include the ones that are flowers)
Only II follows (correct: II directly follows from 'Some trees are houses' → by conversion: Some houses are trees ✓; I doesn't follow because the overlap isn't guaranteed)
Both follow (I doesn't follow — see above)
Neither follows (II follows from converse of particular affirmative)

questions.explanation: B is correct. II follows directly from converting 'Some trees are houses' → 'Some houses are trees'. For I: 'All flowers are trees' and 'Some trees are houses' do NOT guarantee the overlap — the 'some trees' that are houses might be entirely different trees from the flowers. So I does NOT follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: No stone is metal. All metals are conductors.
Conclusions: I. No stone is conductor. II. Some conductors are not stones.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (I: No stone is metal; some conductors are metals; we can't say NO stone is conductor — stones could be conductors via another route)
Only II follows (correct: Since all metals are conductors, and no stone is metal → those metals (which are conductors) are not stones. So some conductors (metals) are not stones → II follows ✓)
Both follow (I is too strong — can't conclude 'No stone is conductor')
Neither follows (II follows as shown)

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'All metals are conductors' → metals are a subset of conductors. 'No stone is metal' → stones are outside the metal set. But stones could still be conductors via non-metal paths. So 'No stone is conductor' (I) doesn't follow. However, metals (which are all conductors) are not stones → 'Some conductors (metals) are not stones' → II follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All roses are flowers. All flowers are beautiful.
Conclusions: I. All roses are beautiful. II. All beautiful things are roses.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (correct: All roses→flowers→beautiful: I follows. But 'All beautiful things are roses' is the converse of universal: invalid ✓)
Only II follows (II doesn't follow — flowers and other things can be beautiful without being roses)
Both follow (II is incorrect — universal affirmative converse is invalid)
Neither follows (I clearly follows via transitivity)

questions.explanation: A is correct. I: All roses are flowers + All flowers are beautiful → All roses are beautiful (transitive). II: 'All beautiful things are roses' would be the converse of the chain — invalid in syllogism. Beautiful things include many things that aren't roses (e.g., sunsets). Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some birds are fish. All fish are reptiles.
Conclusions: I. Some birds are reptiles. II. All reptiles are birds.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (correct: Some birds are fish + All fish are reptiles → Some birds are reptiles (I follows). II is invalid converse of universal ✓)
Only II follows (II is an invalid universal conversion)
Both follow (II doesn't follow)
Neither follows (I follows from the chain)

questions.explanation: A is correct. Some birds are fish → (those birds) are reptiles (since all fish are reptiles). So at least 'Some birds are reptiles' follows (I). II says 'All reptiles are birds' — this would require every reptile to be a bird, which doesn't follow from the given statements. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All chairs are tables. No table is a cupboard. Some cupboards are shelves.
Conclusions: I. No chair is a cupboard. II. Some shelves are not tables.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (I: All chairs are tables + No table is cupboard → No chair is cupboard ✓; II: Some cupboards are shelves + No table is cupboard → some shelves (that are cupboards) are not tables; II also follows)
Both I and II follow (correct: I from chairs→tables and no table is cupboard; II because cupboards that are shelves are not tables ✓)
Only II follows (I also follows)
Neither follows (both clearly follow)

questions.explanation: B is correct. I: All chairs are tables; No table is cupboard → No chair is cupboard (all chairs, being tables, cannot be cupboards). II: Some cupboards are shelves; No table is cupboard → those shelves that are cupboards are not tables → Some shelves are not tables. Both conclusions follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some doctors are teachers. Some teachers are engineers.
Conclusions: I. Some doctors are engineers. II. No doctor is an engineer.
Which follows?

options.option_text: Only I follows (I may or may not follow — 'some doctors are teachers' and 'some teachers are engineers' doesn't guarantee overlap)
Only II follows (II says NO doctor is engineer — equally unproven)
Both follow (both are strong claims that can't both be supported)
Neither follows (correct: 'some' + 'some' gives no definite conclusion — overlap may or may not exist; neither I nor II can be confirmed ✓)

questions.explanation: D is correct. When both premises are particular (Some...Some), no definite conclusion follows. The doctors who are teachers may or may not be among the teachers who are engineers. Both I and II are equally uncertain. This is a key syllogism rule: Particular + Particular = No conclusion.

questions.stem:
Statements: All mangoes are fruits. No fruit is a vegetable. All vegetables are healthy.
Conclusion: No mango is a vegetable.
Does this follow?

options.option_text: Does not follow (it clearly does — all mangoes are fruits, no fruit is vegetable → no mango is vegetable)
Follows (correct: All mangoes are fruits + No fruit is vegetable → No mango is vegetable ✓)
Cannot be determined (the logic is straightforward)
Partially follows (syllogism conclusions are binary — they either follow or don't)

questions.explanation: B is correct. All mangoes are fruits (A⊆F). No fruit is a vegetable (F∩V=∅). Therefore no mango is a vegetable (A∩V=∅). The third statement about vegetables being healthy is irrelevant to this conclusion.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some pens are erasers. All erasers are rubbers. No rubber is a sharpener.
Conclusion: Some pens are not sharpeners.
Does this follow?

options.option_text: Does not follow (some pens are erasers → rubbers → not sharpeners: so at least some pens are not sharpeners — it does follow)
Follows (correct: some pens are erasers → all erasers are rubbers → some pens are rubbers; no rubber is sharpener → those pens (rubbers) are not sharpeners → some pens are not sharpeners ✓)
Cannot be determined (the chain is clear enough to conclude)
Follows only if all pens are erasers (the conclusion is particular — 'some' — so partial coverage suffices)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Chain: Some pens → erasers → rubbers (all erasers are rubbers). No rubber is sharpener. → Those pens that are rubbers are not sharpeners → 'Some pens are not sharpeners' follows. The chain creates a guaranteed subset of pens that cannot be sharpeners.
